metadata.title: Logarithm Laws and Expression Simplification
metadata.description: Combine or expand logarithms by applying the product, quotient, and power laws while preserving positive-argument conditions.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop definitions and laws step by step, explain why each transformation is valid, show intermediate calculations and checks, and use targeted practice with changed-value remedial retries.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 10 “Logarithms,” printed pages 297–307. Approved scope: Derive and apply log_a(xy)=log_a x+log_a y, log_a(x/y)=log_a x−log_a y, and log_a(x^r)=r log_a x for positive arguments and an allowed common base. Use these to combine or expand expressions, simplify prime-factorized numbers, and evaluate exact expressions. State that log_a(x+y) generally does not split into a sum; include a counterexample and distinguish a special numerical coincidence from a law. Respect argument positivity throughout.

content.text: Welcome to Logarithm Laws and Expression Simplification. Combine or expand logarithms by applying the product, quotient, and power laws while preserving positive-argument conditions.
The product law says log_a(xy)=log_a(x)+log_a(y), for x>0, y>0 and an allowed common base. It follows because if x=a^u and y=a^v, then xy=a^(u+v); the product of outputs adds their exponents.
The quotient law says log_a(x/y)=log_a(x)−log_a(y) for positive x and y. If x=a^u and y=a^v, then x/y=a^(u−v). The order matters: numerator log minus denominator log.
The power law says log_a(x^r)=r log_a(x) for x>0 and real r. If x=a^u, then x^r=a^(ru), so its logarithm is ru. The positive-x condition keeps real powers and logarithms within the standard domain.
The laws require a common base. log_2(x)+log_3(y) cannot be combined into one product logarithm directly. Change a base first if useful, or keep the terms separate.
Addition inside an argument does not split: log_a(x+y) is not log_a(x)+log_a(y). For instance, log_10(2+3)=log_10(5), while log_10(2)+log_10(3)=log_10(6).
A special coincidence is not a rule. The source discusses log(1+2+3) and log(1)+log(2)+log(3); they happen to match because both arguments reduce to 6, but arbitrary sums do not behave that way.

To expand a logarithm of a product, factor the argument into positive factors. For example log_10(360)=log_10(2^3·3^2·5)=3log_10(2)+2log_10(3)+log_10(5). Prime factorization makes the exponents visible.
To combine a linear combination of logs, reverse the laws. 2log_a(x)−log_a(y)=log_a(x^2/y), provided x>0 and y>0. Check that the entire combined argument remains positive.
Example: simplify log_5(125)+log_5(4)−log_5(20). Combine to log_5(125·4/20)=log_5(25)=2. The domain is valid because all three original arguments are positive.
Example: evaluate log_10(0.04) using log_10(2)=0.3010. Since 0.04=4/100, log(0.04)=2log2−2=0.6020−2=−1.3980. Keep the negative sign; 0.04 is between 0.01 and 0.1.
For reciprocal arguments, log_a(1/x)=−log_a(x) when x>0. This is the quotient law applied to 1/x and the fact log_a(1)=0.

A common error is to move an exponent inside a logarithm without multiplying by it. log_a(x^3)=3log_a(x), not log_a(x). A reverse error is to multiply when the argument is a product: log_a(xy) is a sum, not a product.

If the logarithms appear in a denominator, do not cancel them as though they were variables unless the identity justifies the operation. For example log_a(x)/log_a(y) can be interpreted by change of base under valid conditions, but it is not automatically log_a(x/y).
A reliable routine is: mark the base, check each argument, identify product/quotient/power structure, apply one law at a time, and combine only after verifying positivity.
After simplifying, expand the result back or substitute easy positive values to check the identity. A numerical check can expose a false sum rule, though the domain-aware derivation is the proof.

The laws can be derived from the definition. Let log_a(x)=u and log_a(y)=v. Then x=a^u and y=a^v, so xy=a^(u+v); taking log base a gives log_a(xy)=u+v. The same exponent reasoning proves quotient subtraction and the power coefficient.
A quotient example keeps the order visible: log_2(40/5)=log_2(40)−log_2(5). Since 40/5=8, the difference must equal 3. Reversing the subtraction would give the wrong sign and fail this direct check.

The positive-argument condition applies to each original logarithm. log_a(x)+log_a(y) requires x>0 and y>0. Even if an algebraic product xy is positive, that alone does not prove both original logs existed.

To expand a compound expression, mark its operation tree: powers become coefficients, numerator products become additions, and denominator factors become subtractions. For log_a(x^2 y^3/z), the result is 2log_a(x)+3log_a(y)−log_a(z), with x,y,z all positive.
